2.text: place. Then they saw the other man passing by with a caravan of sledges. The pack-sledges were

3.text: following one behind another in a long file. The old man took his bow and five arrows and killed

4.text: five reindeer one after another, so that five sledges were left without driving-animals. The people

5.text: of the offender had to attach their own driving-reindeer to the sledges, and to walk slowly afoot.

6.text: So the old man had his revenge for the burnt arrow.”

7.text: As to the Maritime Chukchee, I mentioned a feud between the villages

8.text: Luᵋˊren and Yaˊnřa-ñai, which lasted through more than ten generations, and

9.text: has not been smoothed over even at the present time.¹

10.text: SLAVES. — The term for a male slave was puˊrel, and for a female slave

11.text: ñaˊučhɪn. The latter is simply a variation of the word ñeˊus˙qät (“woman”).

12.text: Other synonymes of the word puˊrel are äᵋmuˊlɪn, vɪˊyolɪn, g̣ŭpɪˊlɪn. Properly

13.text: speaking, puˊrel was a captive of another tribe, or perhaps a man of the same

14.text: tribe who was enslaved, in lieu of blood-revenge. I shall treat of this later

15.text: on. Äᵋmuˊlɪn signifies also “weak one,” “weakling,” and is used as an invec-

16.text: tive, especially with the superlative prefix čiq (čiq-äᵋmuˊlɪn, “a very weak one”).

17.text: Vɪˊyolɪn signifies “assistant,” and is used even for some of the benevolent

18.text: spirits. G̣ŭpɪˊlɪn signifies “a working-man,” and is applied to all workers,

19.text: male or female, even those belonging to one’s own family. Nevertheless all

20.text: these terms are used in a contemptuous sense, and may be used as invectives.

21.text: They are applied also to the real slaves almost without discrimination.

22.text: In modern life slaves hardly exist. The remembrance of them, however,

23.text: is fresh. For instance, two of my acquaintaces — one Araˊro, a very rich

24.text: reindeer-breeder of the western tundra; and the other, Aiñanwaˊt — still

25.text: declared themselves to be descendants of captive slaves of Taˊn˙ñɪn origin;

26.text: and even their neighbors sometimes taunted them with the fact, and called

27.text: them poraˊlčɪñɪn (“piece of a slave”). The line of descent was removed several

28.text: generations. Still Aiñanwaˊt asserted that he himself was a Taˊn˙ñɪn, though

29.text: of course even his great-grandfather spoke only Chukchee and lived among

30.text: that tribe. Even the special incantations which Aiñanwaˊt possessed, as does

31.text: almost every Chukchee reindeer-breeder, mentioned his Taˊn˙ñɪn and Aˊtal-

33.text: The tales often make mention of slaves, male and female, taken as

34.text: prisoners of war. The tale of “Eleˊndi and His Sons” gives a detailed des-

35.text: cription of an enslaved prisoner of Aiˊwan origin. The hero vanquishes him

36.text: in single fight. Then, in order to weaken his future powers of resistance and

37.text: to break his spirit, he beats him with a heavy club all over the muscles and

38.text: fleshy parts of the body. After that he ties him firmly to a pole, and carries

39.text: him away like a log. The slave is suffering, and cries, “I am thirsty!” One

40.text: time they give him water; another time they do not care to do so. When

41.text: brought to the house of the victors, he is made a reindeer-herdsman; and
